Kaka Porowini held that Makoka, Whekoi, Te Waha and Taratikitiki conquered Rawheao and Tupumanawapa; the Māori Land Council rejected the conquest claim for Motatau 5 on 23 November 1905. name: Tawhiri-a-Taka
notes: Kapiti Island — Te Rauparaha's stronghold from ~1822 after Heke Tahutahu-ahi and Heke Tātaramoa from Kāwhia. Pre-eminent base of post-heke Ngāti Toa power, controlling Cook Strait. In 1810 the island was occupied/contested by Muaūpoko; mainland adjacent was Muaūpoko / Ngāti Apa. Toa's arrival is a violent displacement. Source: Taua_settlements_v9.csv, built from the Compendiums folder (Te Ara, Wikipedia, iwi websites, DNZB, Crosby campaign maps) — compendium standard, not primary Coordinate falls outside the map grid; not placed on the terrain. Crosby names this place "Kapiti": P0669 Tawhiri-a-Taka sits on the island 1.6 km from the gazetteer "Kapiti Island" (Island) point, and its notes describe it as Kapiti Island, Te Rauparaha's stronghold; add Kapiti as an alias. Crosby names Taepiro as Te Rauparaha's home, and the gazetteer has "Taepiro" (Historic Site) on the island if a separate pā is wanted.. "It had the advantage of being protected by the stretch of five or six kilometres of sea between it and the mainland at Waikanae." [R. D. name: Whakapara (Taharoa)
coordSrc: Whakapara Marae, 38 Puhipuhi Rd (maorimaps.com), on the Taharoa land beside the Whakapara River
notes: Ngāti Hau kāinga. "Whakapara, also known as Taharoa" (Armstrong, Wai 1040 #P1 p.5). Kahukuri, the Ngāti Hau tupuna, is thought to have occupied land at Whakapara in the mid-1600s (Derby #A61 p.18). The Whakapara branch of Ngāti Hau runs from Te Karu through Taiwhanga (Hoskins #P3 chart). Ngāti Hine also lived at Taharoa: after the Otonga conquest of Te Atihau, Waro of Ngāti Hine lived and cultivated there, with the young Kawiti as his tamaiti (M. P. Kawiti, NMB 6 p.175, in #A61 p.21). Ngāti Manu, or Ngāti Hine, once drove Ngāti Hau off Puhipuhi; Ngāti Hau returned and drove them back to Ruapekapeka (#E67 p.373). Eru Nehua resettled Taharoa c.1861; Whakapara Marae (Te Ihi o Nehua) now stands there. [Ngāti Hau pass 2026-11-04]
